What is a noun?

A noun is a word that names a person, place, animal or thing. For example: 'Emeka' names a person, 'Lagos' names a place, 'goat' names an animal, and 'pencil' names a thing. Nouns can also name ideas we cannot touch, like 'happiness' or 'honesty'. A quick test: if you can put 'the' or 'a' in front of a word and it makes sense (the market, a teacher), it is usually a noun.

Identify the verb in this sentence: Amina sells akara every morning.

Let us find the verb. A verb is an action word, or a word that tells what someone or something does. In 'Amina sells akara every morning', ask: what does Amina do? She sells. So the verb is 'sells'. 'Amina' is a noun (the doer), 'akara' is a noun (what is sold), and 'every morning' tells us when. The action word, the verb, is 'sells'.

Why do we use adjectives?

Good question! We use adjectives to describe nouns, that is, to tell us more about a person, place, animal or thing. Without adjectives, sentences would be plain. Compare: 'I bought a bag' with 'I bought a big, red bag.' The words 'big' and 'red' are adjectives, and they help the listener picture exactly what you mean. So adjectives make our speaking and writing clearer and more interesting.

Pick out the pronoun: Chidi said he would travel to Abuja.

A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun so we do not repeat the noun again and again. In 'Chidi said he would travel to Abuja', instead of saying 'Chidi said Chidi would travel', we replace the second 'Chidi' with 'he'. So the pronoun is 'he'. Other common pronouns are I, you, she, it, we and they.

What are the eight parts of speech?

Every English word belongs to one of eight parts of speech, according to the job it does in a sentence. NOUN — names a person, place, thing or idea: Emeka, Lagos, book, freedom. PRONOUN — replaces a noun: he, she, it, they, we. VERB — shows action or state of being: run, eat, is, become. ADJECTIVE — describes a noun: tall, red, delicious. ADVERB — describes a verb, adjective or another adverb, often telling how, when or where: quickly, yesterday, very. PREPOSITION — shows a relationship of position or time: on, under, before, between. CONJUNCTION — joins words or sentences: and, but, because, although. INTERJECTION — expresses sudden feeling: Wow! Oh! Alas! Remember: a word's part of speech depends on its JOB in that particular sentence, not on the word alone.

What are the types of nouns?

Nouns are grouped into five main types. COMMON nouns name things in general and take a small letter: boy, city, river. PROPER nouns name particular people, places or things and always take a capital letter: Amina, Kano, River Niger, Monday. ABSTRACT nouns name things you cannot touch — ideas, feelings and qualities: love, honesty, freedom, poverty. COLLECTIVE nouns name a group taken as one unit: a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a bunch of bananas, a team of players. CONCRETE nouns name things you can perceive with your senses: table, water, drum. Nouns are also countable (book/books, which you can count) or uncountable (rice, sand, water, which you measure instead). Getting the capital letter right on proper nouns is a frequent exam mark.

What is an adverb and how is it different from an adjective?

An ADJECTIVE describes a NOUN, while an ADVERB describes a VERB, an adjective or another adverb. Compare these two sentences: 'Ngozi is a quick runner' — quick describes the noun 'runner', so it is an adjective. 'Ngozi runs quickly' — quickly describes the verb 'runs', so it is an adverb. Adverbs answer the questions HOW (quickly, carefully, well), WHEN (yesterday, soon, always), WHERE (here, outside, everywhere) and HOW OFTEN (rarely, twice, daily). Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: careful becomes carefully, happy becomes happily. But beware of exceptions: 'fast' and 'hard' stay the same, and 'good' becomes 'well'. So we say 'She sings well', never 'She sings good'.

What is a preposition? Give examples in sentences.

A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence — usually a relationship of position, direction or time. Common ones: in, on, at, under, over, between, beside, from, to, before, after, with. In sentences: 'The book is ON the table' (position). 'Amina travelled TO Ibadan' (direction). 'We resume AFTER the holiday' (time). 'The ball rolled UNDER the chair' (position). 'He shared the mangoes BETWEEN his two sisters' (relationship). A helpful trick: many prepositions describe where a lizard can go relative to a wall — on it, under it, over it, beside it, behind it, near it. Note the fixed Nigerian-exam favourites: we say 'good AT mathematics', 'married TO someone', and 'congratulate someone ON success'.

What are conjunctions and how do I use them?

A conjunction is a joining word — it links words, phrases or whole sentences. COORDINATING conjunctions join items of equal weight: and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor. Examples: 'Bola AND Tunde came to school.' 'I was tired, BUT I finished my homework.' 'Will you take rice OR beans?' SUBORDINATING conjunctions join a main idea to a dependent one, often showing reason, time or condition: because, although, when, while, if, since, unless, until. Examples: 'We stayed indoors BECAUSE it was raining.' 'ALTHOUGH he was tired, he read his book.' 'Call me WHEN you arrive.' Conjunctions turn short choppy sentences into flowing ones, which examiners reward in composition — instead of 'It rained. We stayed inside.' write 'We stayed inside because it rained.'

Identify the part of speech of each word in: The clever girl quickly answered.

Let us take the sentence word by word, asking what job each word does. THE — an article (a special kind of determiner, sometimes classed with adjectives) pointing to a particular girl. CLEVER — an adjective, because it describes the noun 'girl'. GIRL — a noun, naming a person; it is the subject of the sentence. QUICKLY — an adverb, because it describes HOW the action was done, and notice the -ly ending. ANSWERED — a verb, the action word, in the past tense. So the pattern is: article, adjective, noun, adverb, verb. The method to use every time: find the verb (the action) first, then ask who or what did it (the noun or pronoun subject), then check what the remaining words describe.

Can the same word be different parts of speech?

Yes — and this is why you must always look at the word's JOB in the sentence, never memorise words as belonging to one class. Take the word 'water'. In 'The WATER is cold', it names a thing, so it is a noun. In 'Please WATER the flowers', it is an action, so it is a verb. Take 'well'. In 'She sings WELL', it describes the verb, so it is an adverb. In 'They drew water from the WELL', it names a thing, so it is a noun. Another: in 'Book a seat' book is a verb, while in 'Read the book' it is a noun. So when an exam asks for the part of speech of an underlined word, read the whole sentence and ask: what work is this word doing HERE?

What are the types of pronouns?

Pronouns replace nouns so we do not repeat them awkwardly. PERSONAL pronouns stand for people or things: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (as subjects) and me, him, her, us, them (as objects). POSSESSIVE pronouns show ownership: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. REFLEXIVE pronouns point back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves, themselves — as in 'She cooked the rice herself.' DEMONSTRATIVE pronouns point out: this, that, these, those. INTERROGATIVE pronouns ask questions: who, whom, whose, which, what. RELATIVE pronouns join clauses: who, whom, whose, which, that — as in 'The boy WHO won the prize is my friend.' Without pronouns we would write 'Emeka took Emeka's book because Emeka needed Emeka's book' instead of the natural version.
